title: Interval training's best-supported effect is on lean mass, not fat: thirty-six trials, graded [trials, grade_ffm, grade_bf]
teaser: Across thirty-six randomized trials in adults, interval training reduced body fat percentage by 1.53 points and raised fat-free mass by 0.51 kg. [trials, bf_all, ffm_all] The fat result is graded low certainty. [grade_bf] The lean-mass result is graded high, and it hangs on a single trial. [grade_ffm, ffm_loo]
hook: Interval training is sold on fat loss. [-] Pool the trials, rate how far each result can be trusted, and the order flips. [grade_ffm, grade_bf]
populationPanel: Who was studied: 1,130 adults with a mean age of 26.27 years, across thirty-six randomized trials lasting 3 to 15 weeks. [sample, trials] Most were inactive and overweight or obese, so the findings describe that group best. [lim_population] Children, teenagers and people with a known disease were left out. [excluded]

sections.heading: What the pooled trials show
paragraphs: Compared with no exercise, interval training in these adults reduced fat mass by 1.86 kg (95% CI 2.55 to 1.18) and body fat percentage by 1.53 points (95% CI 2.13 to 0.92). [fm_all, bf_all] Fat-free mass, the weight of everything in the body that is not fat, went up by 0.51 kg. [ffm_all]

Then the authors rated how far each result can be trusted, using a system called GRADE. [grade_ffm] Fat-free mass: high. [grade_ffm] Fat mass: moderate. [grade_fm] Body fat percentage: low. [grade_bf] The body-fat trials disagreed with one another heavily; the fat-free-mass trials did not. [heterogeneity_bf, ffm_no_het]

sections.heading: How sure is the lean-mass number?
paragraphs: The 95% confidence interval for fat-free mass runs from 0.06 kg to 0.95 kg. [ffm_all] At its weak end that is 0.06 kg, an amount no bathroom scale would register. [ffm_all] High certainty here means the trials agree that the average effect is above zero. [grade_ffm, ffm_no_het] It does not mean the effect is big. [-]

sections.heading: What most summaries miss
paragraphs: Take one trial out of the pool and the lean-mass effect is gone: the estimate becomes 0.46 kg lost, with an interval from 1.38 kg lost to 0.44 kg gained. [ffm_loo] So the result graded most certain also rests on a single study. [ffm_loo, grade_ffm]

The second surprise is which kind of training did what. [-] Only cycling raised fat-free mass in these trials, by 0.63 kg (95% CI 0.17 to 1.09). [ffm_cycling] Running did not. [ffm_only_cycling] Overground running showed the widest drop in body fat percentage, 2.80 points (95% CI 3.89 to 1.71), but that is the low-certainty outcome. [bf_overground, grade_bf] Treadmill running did not clearly change fat mass at all: its interval runs from 2.82 kg lost to 0.62 kg gained. [fm_treadmill]

sections.heading: The pattern in the programmes
paragraphs: Across outcomes the same settings kept landing on the favourable side: more than 8 weeks, three sessions a week, work bursts under 60 seconds, rests of 90 seconds or less, and moving during the rest. [recipe] These come from comparing subgroups of trials, not from testing one setting directly against another, so treat them as leads. [subgroups]

sections.heading: A related idea
paragraphs: The authors note an earlier pooled analysis that found no clear effect of cycling on fat mass in overweight and obese adults. [wewege] They also raise a practical point: heavier bodies load the joints differently when running, which is one reason cycling may suit some people better whatever the averages say. [joints]

limitations: Most trials enrolled inactive adults who were overweight or obese. [lim_population] The results may not carry over to people who already train. [lim_population]
The trials disagreed with each other, most of all on body fat percentage, which is why that result is graded low. [lim_heterogeneity, grade_bf]
Body composition was measured with different tools from trial to trial, from skinfold calipers to DEXA scans. [lim_methods]
The fat-free-mass result disappears when a single trial is removed. [lim_loo]
takeaways: If lean mass is the aim, the supported combination in these trials was cycling intervals, three sessions a week, for more than 8 weeks. [ffm_cycling, ffm_3wk, ffm_over8]
Keep work bursts to 60 seconds or less: longer bursts showed no clear gain in fat-free mass, with an interval from 2.28 kg lost to 0.57 kg gained. [ffm_le60, ffm_gt60]
Keep moving during the rest. [ffm_active] Standing still between bursts showed no clear gain in fat-free mass. [ffm_passive]
Two sessions a week did not clearly change body fat percentage; three did. [bf_2wk, bf_3wk]

slides.heading: Intervals are sold on fat loss. Thirty-six trials, graded, tell it differently. [trials, grade_bf, grade_ffm]
What changed [-]
slides.body: In adults, interval training reduced body fat percentage by 1.53 points and raised fat-free mass by 0.51 kg, compared with no exercise. [bf_all, ffm_all]

slides.heading: The grades run backwards [-]
slides.body: Certainty for the lean-mass result: high. [grade_ffm] For body fat percentage: low. [grade_bf] The claim that gets the attention has the weaker evidence. [grade_bf, grade_ffm]

slides.heading: And the strong one is fragile [-]
slides.body: Remove a single trial and the lean-mass gain becomes 0.46 kg lost, with an interval from 1.38 kg lost to 0.44 kg gained. [ffm_loo]

carousel.caption: Thirty-six randomized trials of interval training in adults, pooled and graded. [trials] Body fat percentage fell by 1.53 points, at low certainty. [bf_all, grade_bf] Fat-free mass rose by 0.51 kg, at high certainty, though the result depends on one trial. [ffm_all, grade_ffm, ffm_loo] Full read and simulator at the link in bio. [-]
